addressed-o-2303-01469.title: Consistency Models
addressed-o-2303-01469.summary: Matching consistency-loss limits does not establish a useful data-learning objective with unequal teacher and student parameters. The authors’ follow-up removes the teacher EMA and provides the corrected training justification, while retaining the original loss-approximation identity.

checks.location: The discussion after Theorem 2 motivates consistency training with a moving-average teacher from the CT/CD loss approximation as the discretization is refined.
checks.claim: The discussion after Theorem 2 motivates consistency training with a moving-average teacher from the CT/CD loss approximation as the discretization is refined.
checks.explanation: Two objectives can agree while both lose the information needed to learn the data distribution. With unequal teacher and student parameters, the common limiting loss can depend only on their disagreement. The authors’ follow-up explicitly identifies this failure of the training argument; it does not refute Theorem 2’s loss-approximation identity.
checks.demonstration: Let the data distribution be a point mass at $\xi$, with perturbed observations $x_t=\xi+tz$, $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$. Put $a=\sigma_{\min}>0$ and define $$f_\theta(x,t)=\frac atx+\left(1-\frac at\right)\theta.$$ Use $N$ equally spaced noise levels on $[a,T]$, with $T>a$, squared loss and unit weighting. The exact score is $-(x-\xi)/t^2$, so one Euler step from $t+\Delta t$ to $t$ maps $\xi+(t+\Delta t)z$ exactly to $\xi+tz$. The two discrete losses therefore coincide in this example. Writing $b(t)=1-a/t$, their student-minus-teacher residual is $b(t+\Delta t)(\theta-\xi)-b(t)(\theta^--\xi)$. Consequently, for fixed unequal parameters, $$\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{\mathrm{CT}}^N=\lim_{N\to\infty}L_{\mathrm{CD}}^N=\frac1{T-a}\int_a^T b(t)^2\,dt\;(\theta-\theta^-)^2.$$ The limit is independent of the data location $\xi$. Matching it therefore does not establish a useful data-learning objective.
checks.repair: For consistency training, set the teacher’s parameters to $\theta^-=\operatorname{stopgrad}(\theta)$ at every update. This removes the teacher's exponential moving average (EMA) while retaining the detached target. In the same example, write the grid points as $t_1=a,\ldots,t_N=T$ and differentiate only through the student: $$\nabla_\theta L_N=\frac2{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}b(t_{i+1})[b(t_{i+1})-b(t_i)](\theta-\xi).$$ A Riemann-sum limit gives $$\lim_{N\to\infty}(N-1)\nabla_\theta L_N=\left(1-\frac aT\right)^2(\theta-\xi),$$ a positive multiple of the gradient toward the true data location. This proves that the correction restores the learning signal in the exhibited model. For general models, the appropriate justification is the gradient-limit result in the original Theorem 6, under its regularity assumptions and explicit stop-gradient equality, rather than equality of unscaled loss limits. The authors’ follow-up makes this correction; EMA used only for evaluation or for consistency distillation is a separate choice.
checks.scope: The correction addresses the moving-average-teacher justification following Theorem 2. In the scalar example it restores a data-dependent rescaled gradient. Theorem 2's loss identity remains valid, and the original matched-teacher Theorem 6 supplies a gradient-limit result under its own regularity assumptions. Neither the scalar calculation nor agreement of the losses proves universal convergence of consistency training.
checks.title: Agreement of loss limits does not justify a moving-average teacher
checks.claimContext: Theorem 2 compares a consistency-distillation loss $L_{\mathrm{CD}}^N$ and a consistency-training loss $L_{\mathrm{CT}}^N$ on a grid of $N$ noise levels, whose maximum spacing is $\Delta t$. Here $\theta$ denotes the student parameters, $\theta^-$ the teacher parameters, and $\phi$ the score-model parameters used for distillation. The discussion uses their fine-grid agreement to motivate a moving-average teacher. The displayed loss approximation is the theorem's actual claim; the defect is the inference that the common limit remains a useful training objective when $\theta^-\ne\theta$.
checks.whyItMatters: An asymptotic loss identity does not certify that its gradient learns the data. Matching the teacher’s value to the current student while detaching its gradient removes the demonstrated mismatch between parameter agreement and data recovery.
checks.checkedLocation: Original Theorem 2 and following discussion, PDF p. 6; original Theorem 6, p. 22. Follow-up Section 3.2 and Proposition 1, pp. 5–6.

addressed-o-2303-01469.plainExplanation: The original loss approximation does not establish that the limiting objective remains useful when teacher and student parameters differ. review-iarc-037.title: BernNet: Learning Arbitrary Graph Spectral Filters via Bernstein Approximation

checks.location: Proposition2.1 and Lemma3.1: Bernstein approximation versus exact positive representation; Section2 Proposition2.1 complete proof; Section3.3 Lemma3.1 and its use
checks.claim: Proposition2.1 and Lemma3.1: Bernstein approximation versus exact positive representation; Section2 Proposition2.1 complete proof; Section3.3 Lemma3.1 and its use
checks.explanation: Every Bernstein basis polynomial is strictly positive at an interior point of $[0,1]$. A nonnegative combination can therefore vanish there only if every coefficient is zero. This excludes a nonzero polynomial with an interior zero at every finite expansion degree. BernNet can still approximate such a polynomial uniformly.
checks.demonstration:
Let $p(x)=(x-\tfrac12)^2$. It is a degree-$2$ polynomial with $0\leq p(x)\leq\tfrac14$ on $[0,1]$, so it satisfies the lemma. Its degree-$2$ Bernstein coefficients are
$$p(x)=\tfrac14 b_0^2(x)-\tfrac14 b_1^2(x)+\tfrac14 b_2^2(x).$$
Degree elevation cannot remove the obstruction. For any finite $N$, every $b_k^N(\tfrac12)$ is strictly positive. If $p=\sum_{k=0}^N c_kb_k^N$ with $c_k\geq0$, then $p(\tfrac12)=0$ forces all $c_k=0$, contradicting $p(0)=\tfrac14$. Thus $g(\lambda)=p(\lambda/2)$ is also a valid response in $[0,1]$ that the claimed finite nonnegative expansion cannot reproduce exactly.

Approximation behaves differently. The Bernstein approximant of this example satisfies $B_Np(x)=p(x)+x(1-x)/N$, so its uniform error is $1/(4N)$. The interior zero is approached without ever being represented exactly.
checks.repair:
Replace Lemma 3.1 and the ensuing exact-filter-class claim by the approximation statement already supported by Proposition 2.1. For continuous $h:[0,2]\to[0,1]$, use $\theta_k=h(2k/K)$. The Bernstein basis is nonnegative and sums to one, so these coefficients produce a response in $[0,1]$ and the responses converge uniformly to $h$. If $L=U\Lambda U^\top$ is the normalized graph Laplacian, then
$$\|[p_K(L/2)-h(L)]x\|_2\leq\sup_{\lambda\in[0,2]}|p_K(\lambda/2)-h(\lambda)|\,\|x\|_2\longrightarrow0.$$
This correction keeps BernNet and its approximation guarantee intact. Exact representation can instead be stated for polynomials that already have nonnegative Bernstein coefficients. A theorem for strictly positive polynomials would also need to allow a sufficiently large expansion degree, rather than retain degree $K$.
checks.scope: The example satisfies the lemma and the required filter range $[0,1]$. It refutes exact polynomial representation at every finite expansion degree. Proposition 2.1 and the limiting spectral approximation of $h(L)x$ remain valid.
checks.verificationNote: The exact-representation lemma fails; replacing it by the proved uniform-approximation statement repairs the affected justification.
checks.claimContext: Lemma 3.1 claims that every degree-$K$ polynomial nonnegative on $[0,1]$ has a degree-$K$ Bernstein expansion with nonnegative coefficients. Section 3.3 uses this to claim that BernNet represents every valid polynomial filter exactly.
checks.contextBefore: BernNet uses Bernstein basis functions to parameterize graph spectral filters. Proposition 2.1 establishes convergence to any continuous response $h:[0,2]\to[0,1]$ as the degree grows. Lemma 3.1 adds a stronger exact-representation assertion.
checks.title: Nonnegative Bernstein coefficients approximate every valid filter but do not represent every polynomial exactly
checks.whyItMatters: Nonnegative Bernstein coefficients are sufficient for a nonnegative filter, but the lemma treats them as necessary. A valid response with an exact interior zero can fall outside every finite nonnegative Bernstein expansion while remaining uniformly approximable.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.3, Lemma 3.1 and following exact-filter claim, PDF p.6; Proposition 2.1, PDF p.3

checks.demonstration: The printed proof applies a triangle inequality to its squared-MMD notation, which is not generally a metric. Reconstructed the conclusion directly: changing theta in the cross-kernel term changes its expectation by at most 2 E[L]||delta theta||; changing both generated arguments in the generated/generated term contributes at most 2 E[L]||delta theta||. Gaussian kernels are globally Lipschitz in either argument. checks.location: Appendix B.2 Theorem 5(a), Eq.33 and strengthened Eq.29
checks.claim: A lower-tail event with cutoff above its mean is exponentially unlikely, producing a tighter CES power bound.
checks.explanation: An event whose cutoff is above the expectation need not be rare. A bounded independent example with a strictly increased alternative mean gives an exact detection probability below the proposed lower bound.
checks.demonstration:
Write $h_1,\ldots,h_m$ for independent token entropies, $\bar h$ for their average, and $h_{\max}$ for their maximum. The reference cumulative distribution is $F_0$, the alternative distribution is $F_1$, and $\mu_1=\mathbb E_{F_1}h_i$. The score is $\mathrm{CES}=\sqrt{F_0(\bar h)F_0(h_{\max})}$. For a threshold $c$, the proof uses $\mathrm{CES}\ge F_0(\bar h)$ to bound the probability of missing the threshold by a lower-tail probability of $\bar h$. That reduction is useful only when the resulting entropy cutoff lies below $\mu_1$. Equation (33) instead explicitly places it above $\mu_1$ and then applies a lower-tail concentration bound.

An example satisfies every hypothesis of Theorem 5(a), including an upward shift in the mean. Take vocabulary size $d=3$, so the permitted entropy interval $[0,\log 3]$ contains $[0,1]$. Let $F_0$ be uniform on $[0,1]$, and let $h_i$ independently equal one with probability $11/20$ and zero otherwise. Thus $\mu_0=1/2$, $\mu_1=11/20$, and the alternative right endpoint is $\zeta_1=1$. Choose $m=100$, $\mu=27/50$, and $\zeta=9/10$. These choices give

$$\mu<\mu_1,\qquad \zeta<\zeta_1,\qquad c=\sqrt{F_0(\mu)F_0(\zeta)}=\sqrt{243/500}\approx0.697137>F_0(\mu_1)=0.55.$$

Let $K=\sum_{i=1}^{100}h_i$. When $K>0$, the maximum is one and $\mathrm{CES}=\sqrt{K/100}$; when $K=0$, the score is zero. Therefore the exact detection probability is

$$\Pr(\mathrm{CES}\ge c)=\Pr(K\ge49)=\sum_{k=49}^{100}\binom{100}{k}\left(\frac{11}{20}\right)^k\left(\frac9{20}\right)^{100-k}\approx0.904048.$$

The extra exponential term in Equation (29) yields a lower bound of approximately $0.972331$, exceeding that exact probability. This is not a floating-point ambiguity: the binomial sum is a rational number below $181/200=0.905$, whereas the proposed lower bound exceeds $31/32=0.96875$. To certify the latter inequality, use $c>0.697$, $\log3<1.099$, and

$$\frac{200(c-0.55)^2}{(\log3)^2}>\frac72,\qquad e^{7/2}>32.$$

Both exponential comparisons are certified by finite positive Taylor sums in the accompanying control. Equation (29) places $\mu_1$ inside the inverse-CDF parentheses, while Equation (33) places it outside. For this example $F_0^{-1}(u)=u$ at both relevant arguments, so either reading gives the same contradiction.

The problem is limited to the extra concentration term. Equation (28) comes from a valid union bound for the sample mean and maximum. The consistency argument in part (c) cites Equation (28), so this example does not refute the basic power guarantee or consistency under that part's stricter separation assumptions.

This is an exact finite-sample contradiction at $m=100$; neither a central-limit approximation nor an interchange of limits is used. The Bernoulli alternative is admissible as an entropy distribution: with $d=3$, every entropy in $[0,1]$ is attainable by a probability vector because $1<\log3$. The example has $\mu_1>\mu_0$, as well as the threshold conditions in part (a). It does not meet part (c)'s separate endpoint-separation condition because both right endpoints equal one.
checks.repair:
A sufficient local correction is to remove the extra minimum term in Equation (29) and retain Equation (28). To justify the stronger route instead, set $c=\sqrt{F_0(\mu)F_0(\zeta)}\in(0,1]$, let $a=F_0^{-1}(c)=\inf\{x:F_0(x)\ge c\}$, and require $a<\mu_1$. This condition reverses the direction used in the paper. Since a CDF is right-continuous, $F_0(a)\ge c$, so $F_0(\bar h)<c$ implies $\bar h<a$, including when $F_0$ has atoms. Because $h_{\max}\ge\bar h$, the score satisfies $\mathrm{CES}\ge F_0(\bar h)$. Hence, for independent $h_i\in[0,\log d]$,

$$\Pr(\mathrm{CES}<c)\le\Pr(\bar h<a)\le\exp\!\left[-\frac{2m(\mu_1-a)^2}{(\log d)^2}\right].$$

Intersecting this valid bound with the union-bound argument yields

$$\Pr(\mathrm{CES}\ge c)\ge1-\min\!\left\{\exp\!\left[-\frac{2m(\mu_1-a)^2}{(\log d)^2}\right],\ F_1(\zeta)^m+\exp\!\left[-\frac{2m(\mu_1-\mu)^2}{(\log d)^2}\right]\right\}.$$

Retain the theorem's conditions $\mu<\mu_1$ and $\zeta<\zeta_1$ when combining the two bounds. The inverse-CDF placement must also be made consistent: the exponent contains $(\mu_1-F_0^{-1}(c))^2$. This correction proves a stronger bound in a different threshold regime; it does not justify the originally printed regime $c>F_0(\mu_1)$. The remaining exponential error bounds concern independent bounded entropies and the exact reference CDF. To apply part (c), both intervals $\mu\in(\mu_0,\mu_1)$ and $\zeta\in(\zeta_0,\zeta_1)$ must be nonempty. The counterexample does not establish those conditions for empirical token sequences or an estimated reference CDF.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns the added term in Theorem 5(a), Equation (29), and its Equation (33) proof. Equation (28) and the part (c) argument based on it are not refuted. No numerical performance claim is inferred from this example.

checks.claim: Distribution-free KS Type-I validity survives serial dependence.
checks.explanation: Identical continuous marginals do not determine the null distribution of an empirical CDF under dependence. Four repeats of one uniform draw in each of two independent groups give KS distance one with probability one under equal marginals.
checks.demonstration:
Section 4.1 pools all token entropies within each faithful or hallucinated group, separately for each model–dataset pair. Thus tokens are the observations entered into the two-sample empirical CDFs, while the generation is the within-sequence dependence block. The null needed by ordinary token-level KS calibration treats all those token observations as independent. Equality of the two marginal token distributions does not supply that independence. Figure 2's permuted-null label does not specify an exchangeable whole-generation design and cannot establish the general assertion in Appendix E.3.

The conditional independence assumption is stated explicitly in Assumption 1, and Appendix E.3 begins by acknowledging that the KS test assumes independent observations. Its later interpretation nevertheless claims that distribution-free calibration preserves Type-I error under the observed serial dependence. Here, distribution-free means independence of the continuous marginal distribution within the independent-sample model; it does not mean independence of the joint dependence structure.

A two-sample null example matches the form of the distribution comparison. Let $U$ and $V$ be independent uniform random variables on $[0,1]$. Set $X_1=\cdots=X_4=U$ and $Y_1=\cdots=Y_4=V$. Both groups have the same uniform marginal distribution, and the groups are independent of one another. Within each group the observations are perfectly dependent. If $\widehat F_X$ and $\widehat F_Y$ denote their empirical CDFs, then

$$D_{4,4}=\sup_t|\widehat F_X(t)-\widehat F_Y(t)|=1\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

Indeed, $U\ne V$ with probability one, and between their two values one empirical CDF is one while the other is zero. Under the continuous independent-sample KS calibration, the probability of $D_{4,4}=1$ is

$$\frac{2}{\binom84}=\frac1{35}<0.05.$$

Only the two orderings with all four observations of one group before all four of the other have this distance. Thus the ordinary 5% test rejects with probability one under this dependent null. Correct marginal distributions alone cannot justify its calibration.

This construction does not estimate the Type-I error in the paper's data, and its strong dependence is not being attributed to those data. It disproves the stated general justification. Small lag-one autocorrelation does not itself supply a null law for the KS statistic, nor does the effective-sample-size formula used for a sample mean establish that law. The iid calibration theorems retain their stated assumptions; the affected claim is the interpretation of the dependence diagnostics.
checks.repair:
Keep the distribution-free KS guarantee under its independent-sample null, and state the autocorrelation measurements as diagnostics. Preserving the two-sample pooled-token statistic requires a calibration unit that preserves dependence within a generation.

One sufficient finite-sample design is a permutation test on whole generations. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_N$ denote complete entropy sequences, including their lengths. Assume that, under the null, the generation labels are exchangeable conditional on the pooled sequences and fixed group sizes. For each permitted label assignment $g$ in a finite set $\mathcal P$, recompute exactly the same two-sample statistic $T(g)$ after pooling the sequences assigned to each group. If $g_0$ is the observed assignment, use

$$p_{\rm perm}=\frac{\#\{g\in\mathcal P:T(g)\ge T(g_0)\}}{|\mathcal P|}.$$

Conditional on the pooled sequences, $g_0$ is uniform on $\mathcal P$. At most $\lfloor\alpha|\mathcal P|\rfloor$ assignments can have this upper-tail rank at most $\alpha$; ties make the test conservative. Therefore $\Pr(p_{\rm perm}\le\alpha)\le\alpha$. Internal token dependence is preserved because the complete sequence moves as one unit. Any data-dependent centering or other preprocessing must be recomputed by the same rule for every assignment.

This repair tests exchangeability of complete generations, a stronger null than equality of token marginals alone. If labels are not exchangeable across lengths or prompts, stratification requires exchangeability within the chosen strata; if several generations share dependent sampling units, the whole independent block must move together. The source does not establish these conditions for its correctness labels. A mean-based effective-sample-size adjustment or a low lag-one autocorrelation cannot replace that missing argument. The minimal justified correction is to remove the unconditional Type-I guarantee while retaining the iid results and measured KS distances.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns the Type-I interpretation in Appendix E.3. The counterexample does not estimate the error rate in the reported token sequences and does not contradict the theorems that explicitly assume iid observations.
checks.whyItMatters: An independence diagnostic cannot by itself certify the false-positive rate of an iid KS test. A dependent-data guarantee needs a null model or a calibration design that accounts for whole-sequence dependence.
checks.title: Distribution-free KS calibration does not justify Type-I control under serial dependence

checks.claim: Localized target-trajectory-only performance bound
checks.explanation: The bound is false even at $c=0$ with a single source and exact evaluation. Reward differences on a source policy’s continuation can make TRAM reject a target-optimal action, although all rewards on the target-optimal trajectory agree.
checks.demonstration:
Take one source task and one target task with the same finite deterministic dynamics and discount $\gamma=0.9$. A forced action at a root state gives reward zero and moves to $u$. At $u$, action $\mathrm{good}$ gives reward zero and moves to $v$, whereas $\mathrm{safe}$ gives reward $0.5$ and terminates. At $v$, action $\mathrm{finish}$ gives reward $1$ and terminates in either task. The remaining action, $\mathrm{bad}$, terminates with reward $100$ in the source and $-100$ in the target. All rewards are bounded. Use the allowed choice $c=0$ and the zero risk functional, which is $0$-Lipschitz.

The source-optimal policy $\pi_j^*$ takes $\mathrm{good}$ at $u$ and $\mathrm{bad}$ at $v$: its source value for $\mathrm{good}$ at $u$ is $0.9\cdot100=90>0.5$. Evaluate this policy exactly under the target reward. Its target action values at $u$ are
$$Q_T^{\pi_j^*}(u,\mathrm{good})=0.9(-100)=-90,\qquad Q_T^{\pi_j^*}(u,\mathrm{safe})=0.5.$$
TRAM therefore selects $\mathrm{safe}$ at $u$. The target-optimal policy instead takes $\mathrm{good}$ and then $\mathrm{finish}$.

Starting from the same forced root action in both cases gives
$$Q_T^*(\mathrm{root},a)=0.9^2\cdot1=0.81,\qquad Q_T^{\mathrm{TRAM}}(\mathrm{root},a)=0.9\cdot0.5=0.45.$$
This is a comparison of $Q$ values at a common initial state-action pair. Every reward on the target-optimal trajectory is identical in the two tasks, so its localized discrepancy is $\Delta_{\pi^*}^{(T,j)}=0$. The choice $c=0$ also removes every risk and stitching-risk term. Equation (4.6) consequently bounds the positive gap $0.81-0.45=0.36$ by zero. The missing reward mismatch lies along the source policy whose target evaluation determines TRAM's choice.
checks.repair:
A reward-only replacement is valid under common finite dynamics, bounded rewards, $0\leq\gamma<1$, exact target evaluation, source-optimal policies $\pi_j^*$, and $c=0$:
$$Q_T^{\pi^*}(s,a)-Q_T^{\pi_T}(s,a)
\leq\min_j\{\Delta_{\pi^*}^{(T,j)}(s,a)+\Delta_{\pi_j^*}^{(T,j)}(s,a)\}.$$
To see the policy-improvement step, put $q(s,a)=\max_jQ_T^{\pi_j^*}(s,a)$ and choose $\pi_T(s)\in\arg\max_a q(s,a)$. Each source policy’s target value satisfies $V_T^{\pi_j^*}(s)\leq\max_a q(s,a)$, hence the target Bellman operator obeys $\mathcal T_T^{\pi_T}q\geq q$. Its monotone contraction iterates converge to $Q_T^{\pi_T}$, giving $Q_T^{\pi_T}\geq q$.

For each source, add and subtract the two source-task values:
$$Q_T^{\pi^*}-Q_T^{\pi_j^*}
=(Q_T^{\pi^*}-Q_j^{\pi^*})+(Q_j^{\pi^*}-Q_j^{\pi_j^*})+(Q_j^{\pi_j^*}-Q_T^{\pi_j^*}).$$
Source optimality makes the middle term nonpositive; the two remaining fixed-policy differences are bounded by their respective localized discrepancies. This proves the replacement. Bounding each discrepancy by $\|r_T-r_j\|_\infty/(1-\gamma)$ gives the global reward-only term $2\|r_T-r_j\|_\infty/(1-\gamma)$ used in v1. This argument applies to $c=0$; a risk-adjusted extension requires its own policy-improvement result.
checks.scope: The affected results are Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2 of arXiv v2, together with the target-trajectory-only mismatch argument in Appendix B. The earlier v1 global reward bound controls both trajectories through a uniform discrepancy and is not contradicted by this example.

checks.claim: Per-step variance formula
checks.explanation: The first term is a second moment under the normalized occupancy. The second term squares the unnormalized discounted reward sum. Subtracting moments with different normalizations is not a variance: even a constant deterministic reward gives a negative value.
checks.demonstration:
Equation (A.5) gives
$$\sum_{s,a}d(s,a)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=1.$$
Consider a one-state, one-action MDP with a deterministic self-loop, reward $r\equiv1$, and $0<\gamma<1$. Its occupancy is $d(s,a)=1$ and its conditional second moment is $\tilde r(s,a)=1$. Every sampled one-step reward equals one, so its variance is zero. Equation (A.10), however, gives
$$\rho_{\mathrm{var}}(d)=1-\frac1{(1-\gamma)^2}<0.$$
For $\gamma=9/10$, the value is $-99$.

Equation (A.8) does not fix this contradiction. Its symbol $\mathbb E_d$ integrates against $d/(1-\gamma)$, whose total mass is $1/(1-\gamma)$. Thus the preceding identity $\langle d,r\rangle=(1-\gamma)\mathbb E_d[r]$ describes a discounted sum, not a probability expectation. Equation (A.10) combines the normalized second moment with the square of that sum.
checks.repair:
For a normalized occupancy $d$, define the probability law
$$\Pr(S=s,A=a,S'=s')=d(s,a)p(s'\mid s,a).$$
Assume the reward $R=r(S,A,S')$ has a finite second moment. Then
$$\mathbb E R=\langle d,r\rangle,\qquad \mathbb E R^2=\langle d,\tilde r\rangle,$$
so the corrected per-step variance is
$$\rho_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{step}}(d)=\langle d,\tilde r\rangle-\langle d,r\rangle^2
=\mathbb E[(R-\mathbb E R)^2]\geq0.$$
If equation (A.8)'s discounted-sum notation is retained, the same formula is
$$(1-\gamma)\mathbb E_d[R^2]-(1-\gamma)^2\bigl(\mathbb E_d[R]\bigr)^2.$$
Both expressions give zero for every constant reward. They describe the variance of one reward drawn from the discounted occupancy, rather than the variance of an entire discounted return.
checks.scope: The affected expression is the per-step variance entry (R2), equation (A.10), in arXiv v2. Its normalization must agree with equations (A.5) and (A.8). The separate reward-transfer counterexample uses a zero risk functional and does not depend on this variance formula.
checks.title: The per-step variance formula mixes normalized and unnormalized moments
checks.claimContext: Appendix A.3 lists occupancy-based risk functionals. Equation (A.5) defines a normalized discounted occupancy $d$, while equation (A.10) labels its expression as per-step reward variance. Here $0\leq\gamma<1$, $r(s,a)$ is the conditional mean reward, and $\tilde r(s,a)$ is its conditional second moment.
checks.whyItMatters: A deterministic reward stream receives negative local variance, so the expression cannot represent the stated risk measure.
checks.checkedLocation: arXiv v2 · Appendix A.1, equation (A.5); Appendix A.2, equation (A.8); Appendix A.3 (R2), equation (A.10).

then a representation trained purely by
mean-regression motion supervision cannot separate $a_{1}$ from $a_{2}$ above chance.
checks.explanation: Squared-error supervision constrains the composition of encoder and prediction head. It does not prevent the encoder from retaining information ignored by the head. Equal class means therefore do not impose the stated limit on representation-level classification or guarantee a strict mutual-information advantage for another representation.
checks.demonstration:
Let $A$ be a balanced binary label. Given $A=0$, motion $M$ is uniform on $\{-1,1\}$; given $A=1$, it is uniform on $\{-2,2\}$. Let the available context be $X=|M|-1=A$, use encoder $Z=X$, and set the prediction head to $h(Z)=0$. Both conditional motion means are zero, and any predictor $b(X)$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E(M-b(X))^2=\frac52+\mathbb E b(X)^2.$$
Thus the zero head attains the Bayes-optimal regression loss, while $Z$ predicts the label perfectly and $I(Z;A)=1$ bit. No representation can contain strictly more than the label entropy of one bit. This construction also satisfies the Markov-chain premise in the earlier theoretical appendix because $Z$ is a function of $M$.
checks.repair: Limit the obstruction to the statistic supplied to the classifier. If that statistic is only the predicted mean $U=\mathbb E[M\mid X]$ and its conditional distributions are identical in two balanced classes, then its Bayes classification accuracy is $1/2$. In the example, $U=0$ loses the class information, while the full conditional motion distributions differ in variance. This supports a motivation for distributional supervision without a universal claim about encoder information. The v1 appendix already distinguishes these statistics; the current informal proposition should use that narrower scope.
checks.scope: The counterexample concerns the current proposition’s representation-level impossibility and strict information ordering. A classifier receiving only an identical mean statistic has the narrower obstruction. The v1 appendix made that distinction explicitly, while the v3/v4 manuscripts retain the broader main-text proposition without that appendix.
checks.whyItMatters: A limitation of the prediction statistic is not automatically a limitation of every feature learned by the encoder.

checks.explanation: The correction cancels the incoming instruction’s value at the new decision boundary. It does not ensure that this boundary would exist without the interruption. Early termination can change the macro’s duration, endpoint and available continuation. Primitive transition factorization does not imply equality of these macro-boundary laws.
checks.demonstration:
Consider one fully observed agent, terminal state $z$, and discount $\gamma=1/2$. Under instruction $c$, macro $a$ is committed to the two steps $x\to y\to z$. The first reward is zero and the second is one. It does not normally terminate at $y$. At a fresh decision in $y$, the policy instead chooses macro $b$, which moves to $z$ with zero reward. Under instruction $d$, it also chooses $b$.

With instruction frozen at $c$, macro $a$ completes and the value from $x$ is $\gamma=1/2$. If the instruction changes from $c$ to $d$ after the first step, the method interrupts $a$ at $y$. Both fresh-decision continuation values at $y$ are zero, so its correction is

$$\gamma\bigl(V(y,c)-V(y,d)\bigr)=0.$$

The interrupted process then selects $b$ and has value zero. Physical transitions given primitive actions are instruction-independent throughout. The discrepancy comes from replacing continuation of the active macro by a fresh policy decision. An inert second agent can be included without changing the construction.
checks.repair:
For the printed cancellation proof, require the same marginal macro-boundary law in the augmented and frozen problems, including history, endpoint and duration. One sufficient design allows instruction changes only at natural macro boundaries. If $K$ is that common law, the corrected continuation satisfies

$$V(h',d)+\mathbf1\{d\ne c\}\bigl(V(h',c)-V(h',d)\bigr)=V(h',c).$$

Averaging the corrected reward and $\gamma^\tau V(h',c)$ over $K$ then gives the frozen-instruction Bellman operator. With bounded rewards, $0\le\gamma<1$ and macro duration $\tau\ge1$, contraction gives the same fixed-point value. To retain forced interruption during a macro, the counterfactual continuation must instead include the active macro and its remaining execution; substituting a fresh-decision value is insufficient.
checks.scope: The issue concerns equivalence to uninterrupted execution in the frozen-instruction problem. The common-boundary repair proves a restricted equivalence, while the original forced-interruption setting requires additional state and continuation semantics. This argument does not contradict the reported task scores.
checks.whyItMatters: The method is designed to handle instructions arriving during long actions. A value correction must account for the interrupted action’s remaining execution if it is to reproduce the value of uninterrupted behavior.

checks.demonstration:
Assume the two KL divergences are finite and let \(d^*=\log(dP/dQ)\). Direct substitution into the difference of expectations gives
\[U(d^*)=\mathbb E_P\log\frac{dP}{dQ}-\mathbb E_Q\log\frac{dP}{dQ}=D_{\rm KL}(P\Vert Q)+D_{\rm KL}(Q\Vert P).\]

checks.claim: For any endpoint coupling pi that assigns zero mass to the antipodal locus, the bridge makes the conditional law of (X0,X1) given Xt=x absolutely continuous with a smooth density w.r.t. the product Riemannian volume.
checks.explanation: Noise in the intermediate observation does not change an endpoint that is deterministic under the prior. Bayes' rule can produce a density relative to the endpoint coupling without producing one relative to product Riemannian volume. The proof conflates those two reference measures.
checks.demonstration:
Take one token on $\mathcal S^2$, with $X_0$ uniform, $X_1=y$ deterministic, and independent endpoints. The antipodal event $X_0=-y$ has probability zero, so the stated coupling condition holds. Use the paper's positive interior noise schedule.

The event $X_1=y$ has probability one before observing $X_t$. Hence, by disintegration, it still has conditional probability one for $\mathcal L(X_t)$-almost every observation. The conditional endpoint law is therefore supported on
$$\mathcal S^2\times\{y\},$$
a set of zero product Riemannian volume. It cannot have a density relative to that volume.

The correct Bayes expression is
$$d\pi_{t,x}(x_0,x_1)=
\frac{k_t(x\mid x_0,x_1)}{\int k_t(x\mid z_0,z_1)\,d\pi(z_0,z_1)}\,d\pi(x_0,x_1).$$
A positive observation likelihood reweights $\pi$; it does not remove its singular support.
checks.repair: State the reference measure explicitly. Under the existing endpoint assumptions, Bayes' rule gives a posterior density relative to $\pi$, not product volume. If a product-volume density is required, impose an appropriate endpoint-coupling density and prove the relevant smoothness and differentiation bounds. The rectifiability argument must then use those precise conditions; changing the reference measure alone does not prove its remaining steps.
checks.scope: This refutes the universal product-volume posterior-density assertion under the stated endpoint hypotheses. It does not refute the separate full-support property of $X_t$, nor establish that a particular trained velocity field fails to define a valid flow.
checks.whyItMatters: The theorem uses posterior smoothness as a premise for later regularity arguments. A smooth likelihood alone does not supply that premise for arbitrary endpoint laws.
checks.claimContext: The current Theorem 1(ii) claims a smooth conditional density for $(X_0,X_1)$ given an interior bridge observation $X_t=x$. It inherits a coupling condition excluding antipodal pairs, but does not assume the endpoint distribution has a density. Appendix B.3 specifies Riemannian volume as the reference measure.

checks.claim: The local statistic estimates Vprime=E[d]/2 and has concentration about that value.
checks.explanation: The printed pair average estimates twice the defined population variability, so its claimed concentration about that variability fails.
checks.demonstration: Each of the $m(m-1)/2$ summands has mean $2V'(\mathcal C)$. Multiplication by the printed factor $2/[m(m-1)]$ therefore leaves mean $2V'(\mathcal C)$. For one cell containing both rankings in $\mathfrak S_2$, take the uniform distribution. Then $V'=1/4$ and the statistic is $2X(N-X)/[N(N-1)]$ for $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,1/2)$, converging to $1/2$. On $N/4\le X\le3N/4$ its error exceeds $1/8$. This event has probability at least $1-2e^{-N/8}$, whereas Lemma 1 bounds the same error probability by $2e^{-N/64}$ because its cell constant is one. The two bounds contradict each other for large $N$.
checks.repair: Replace the local factor by $1/[m(m-1)]$. Conditional on $m$, the corrected statistic is a degree-two U-statistic with kernel $d/2$. If the cell diameter is $D>0$, Hoeffding gives $\Pr(|\widehat V'-V'|\ge t\mid m)\le2\exp(-8\lfloor m/2\rfloor t^2/D^2)$. For a full-partition oracle statistic, use the kernel $h(\sigma,\sigma')=\tfrac12\sum_{\mathcal C}\mathbf1_{\mathcal C^2}(\sigma,\sigma')d(\sigma,\sigma')/P(\mathcal C)$. Its mean is $\mathcal E'$ and it lies in $[0,\kappa_{\mathcal P}/2]$, so the same U-statistic bound applies. A zero-diameter cell is deterministic and needs no deviation bound. A data-dependent cell denominator requires separate count control.
checks.scope: A factor correction repairs the local estimator, but it does not by itself justify treating the entire empirical cell-weighted statistic as a fixed-kernel U-statistic. The one-cell example already disproves the printed concentration around $\mathcal E'$. It does not decide every later learning rate.

checks.claim: Larger semantic correctness probability than format-validity probability implies format-dominated RL updates.
checks.explanation: The proof compares probability coefficients from two different product-rule decompositions of the same gradient. A larger coefficient does not imply a larger gradient contribution: the derivatives and their alignment also matter. Rescaling a trainable policy coordinate can reverse the comparison without changing either success probability.
checks.demonstration:
Use one prompt and a trajectory consisting of two independent bits. Let
\[
a=\Pr(F=1)=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\operatorname{logit}(0.2)+0.01u),
\qquad
b=\Pr(S=1)=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\operatorname{logit}(0.8)+v).
\]
All four trajectories have positive probability. At \(u=v=0\), \(b=0.8>a=0.2\), and the expected reward is \(J=ab\). Direct differentiation gives
\[
\nabla_{(u,v)}J=(0.00128,\,0.032).
\]
Under Euclidean gradient ascent, the instantaneous changes in the two success probabilities are
\[
\dot a=0.000002048,\qquad \dot b=0.00512.
\]
Semantic success therefore increases \(2{,}500\) times faster than format validity, although the lemma's probability condition holds.
checks.repair:
Retain the exact probability factorizations and state a comparison only under an explicit choice of optimization coordinates. For independent events optimized directly in equally scaled probability coordinates, \(J(a,b)=ab\), so
\[
\partial_aJ=b,\qquad \partial_bJ=a.
\]
Then \(b>a\) does imply the larger format-coordinate update. A neural-policy claim additionally needs assumptions on the parameter derivatives and update metric; the probability ordering by itself supplies neither.
checks.scope: This counterexample addresses the gradient-domination conclusion of Lemma 3.1 and its restatement in Appendix A. The product-rule identities are valid.
checks.title: Success probabilities alone do not determine which policy update is larger

checks.location: AppendixB Proposition5(1), h_i and area decomposition
checks.explanation: The printed height is not real even for an equilateral triangle. Replacing the side by its half length repairs the acute-triangle calculation; unrestricted obtuse triangles require clipped Voronoi geometry.
checks.demonstration:
Take an equilateral triangle of side \(1\). Its circumradius satisfies \(R^2=1/3\), so every printed radicand equals \(-2/3\), despite positive real basin areas.

For an acute triangle the circumcenter lies inside the triangle. The segment from it to a side midpoint is a Voronoi ridge. Pythagoras gives
\[
h_i^2+(u_i/2)^2=R^2.
\]
The wedge for either endpoint has base \(u_i/2\) and height \(h_i\), hence area \(u_i h_i/4\). The six wedges partition the acute triangle. For the equilateral test the corrected height is \(1/(2\sqrt3)\), and \(2\sum_i a_i=\sqrt3/4\), exactly its area.
checks.repair:
For acute triangles use \(h_i=\sqrt{R^2-u_i^2/4}\); the preceding right-triangle and wedge decomposition proves the repaired formula. For arbitrary nondegenerate triangles define the clipped cell directly by
\[
V_i=T\cap\bigcap_j\{x:\|x-v_i\|^2\le\|x-v_j\|^2\},\qquad p_i=\frac{\operatorname{area}(V_i)}{\operatorname{area}(T)}.
\]
Each inequality is a half-plane. These cells cover \(T\), with overlap only on boundaries of area zero, so their areas give the normalized basin distribution without an acute-triangle assumption.
checks.scope: This refutes Appendix B’s formula. It does not refute the general point-cloud Markov construction.
checks.title: The three-point basin-height formula uses a full side in place of a half side
checks.claimContext: Appendix B clips the three Voronoi cells to their Delaunay triangle. Here \(u_i\) is the full side length, \(R\) its circumradius, and the proposed wedge area is \(a_i=u_i h_i/4\), with triangle area \(A=2\sum_i a_i\). No acute-triangle restriction is stated.

checks.demonstration:
For an equilateral three-point model let each off-diagonal area weight be \(b>0\), and take the permitted diagonal weight \(a=b/10\). Then
\[
P=\frac1{21}\begin{pmatrix}1&10&10\\10&1&10\\10&10&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\operatorname{spec}(P)=\{1,-3/7,-3/7\}.

The nonconstant eigenvectors contract by \(3/7\) in modulus, giving gap \(4/7\). The printed expression gives \(10/7\). Positive diagonal entries make this example aperiodic.

It achieves full coverage on five domains; on Robot, its selected heuristics exceeded the SLURM wall-clock limit on the 8 largest problems and the remaining 12 were all solved.
Gemini 3 Flash is the second-best model at 4,346 median nodes; Gemini 3 Pro follows at 14,746 nodes; Gemini 2.0 Flash and Gemini 2.5 Pro are substantially weaker at approximately 48,600 and 51,200 nodes respectively.
Model variance is high.

Four of the nine models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, and GPT-5.2) produced 20 candidate heuristics for every domain, but in five of six domains none of their 20 candidates passed the local selection step.
GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5 retained surviving candidates only on Depots; GPT-5 and GPT-5.2 only on Towers.

checks.location: Section4.3 Clean Control, work/text/153652.txt line378; context Table3 and Section3.4 three-seed/20-task evaluation
checks.claim: An observed baseline/control equality of5% implies no permission-prior degradation from Bash distillation, and therefore the experimental bias is attributable entirely to teacher trait inheritance.
checks.explanation: The paper defines a task-level event rate, evaluates 20 tasks, and averages three seeds. Equality of reported baseline/control estimates at 5% is equality of finite outcomes, not equality of their underlying event probabilities. To test whether the entire-causation inference follows, consider the admissible policy model in which each task/seed has chmod-first probability .05 for baseline and .15 for benign-distilled control; all other outcomes select an alternative first permission-modifying command. One event among 20 has probability 20*p*(1-p)^19. Both models can produce exactly one event in each of three seeds, hence the same reported 5%, with joint probability .00013755869001423921>0 despite a true generic control shift of 10 percentage points. Safe training-data filtering places no mathematical equality constraint on these evaluation policies. Even under a favorable iid pooling assumption, 3/60 has a 95% exact interval approximately [.01043,.13924]; an actual same-task/seed dependence model could require different inference. Moreover a net equality of aggregate rates would not uniquely identify every causal mechanism or taskwise change.

The Llama 3B $\rightarrow$ Llama 8B configuration produced no measurable transfer (student bias 5%, matching the baseline exactly), consistent with the API setting’s finding that small-to-large distillation is ineffective. checks.contextAfter: We presented the first empirical evidence of subliminal behavioral transfer in AI agents across two complementary experimental settings. In the API setting, a deletion bias transferred from teacher to student through safe, filtered trajectories containing no explicit deletion content, with student deletion rates reaching 100% under homogeneous distillation. In the Bash setting, a chmod-first bias transferred through an unbounded shell-command interface, with student bias reaching 30%–55% despite full keyword sanitation. These findings have significant implications for AI safety: current practices of filtering training data for explicit unsafe content are insufficient to prevent behavioral bias propagation.

checks.claim: The multiclass observable-data rate holds under the stated margin conditions, including distributions with top-class ties.
checks.explanation: Those conditions ignore zero top-two gaps even when a lower class can win and incur positive regret.
checks.demonstration: On uniform $X\in[0,1]$, set $g=x^2/4$, $P_1=P_2=(1+g)/3$ and $P_3=(1-2g)/3$. The probabilities are positive Lipschitz functions and both positive-gap margin integrals vanish. With $n=m^3$ and cell width $1/m$, the first $\sqrt m$ cells have average gap at most $1/(4m)$. Their label-count laws are within total variation $1/4$ of equal-label counts, under which strict class-three plurality has probability at least $1/3-O(1/m)$. Hence class three wins with probability at least $1/12-O(1/m)$, independent of tie breaking. Integrating its regret gives $\Omega(m^{-3/2})=\Omega(n^{-1/2})$, slower than the claimed $O(n^{-2/3})$.
